title: DriveAgent-R1: Advancing VLM-based Autonomous Driving with Active Perception and Hybrid Thinking
one_liner: DriveAgent-R1 decides when to gather more visual evidence and when to reason from text alone, so driving decisions stay efficient on easy scenes and better grounded on hard scenes.
lead: A driving agent often sees many scenes that are easy to classify quickly, plus a smaller number of scenes where the right action depends on a hard-to-read visual detail. If the system always uses heavy visual checking, it becomes slow. If it never does, it may miss the decisive evidence in complex scenes. DriveAgent-R1 learns a hybrid policy: use fast text-based reasoning on straightforward scenes, and actively call visual tools when uncertainty makes extra evidence worth the time.

problem.h2: The problem: passive perception misses decisive evidence
paras: End-to-end driving systems based on vision and language can reason about high-level maneuvers, but many of them treat perception as passive. They consume the available visual input and then reason from whatever text summary or internal state they already have. That is risky when the scene contains an ambiguous object, an occluded lane marker, or a hard-to-read traffic signal.

A human driver does not handle every scene with the same depth of inspection. Some moments require a quick decision because the situation is clear. Other moments justify an extra look because one visual detail decides whether it is safe to proceed. The paper builds that choice into the agent.

callout.b: The core idea in one sentence.
callout.html: Let the driving agent switch between fast text-only reasoning and tool-based visual checking, so it asks for more evidence only when scene complexity makes that extra cost worthwhile.

steps.b: Step 1: Read the scene and form an initial plan
steps.text: The driving agent processes the current road scene and proposes an action using its standard reasoning path.
The agent judges whether the current scene is simple enough for fast reasoning or uncertain enough to require more evidence.

steps.b: Step 3: Call visual tools when needed
steps.text: On uncertain scenes, the agent invokes active perception tools to inspect the exact parts of the visual field that matter for the decision.
The new visual findings feed back into the driving plan, so the final action is grounded in observed scene details rather than in a coarse summary alone.

steps.b: Step 5: Train the switch with progressive learning
steps.text: A staged training process, including Cascaded RL, teaches when to stay fast and when to pay for deeper checking.

object.h2: What changes: perception becomes an action
paras: The paper changes the role of perception. Instead of treating visual understanding as a fixed precomputed input, DriveAgent-R1 treats evidence gathering as a decision the agent can make during planning. That means the agent chooses not only what action to take on the road, but also whether it needs another perception step before committing.

hidden.name: How much one more visual check would improve the driving decision
paras: The important hidden quantity is evidence value. A visual tool call is helpful only when the extra observation changes the driving decision enough to justify the delay and compute. On a straight open road, evidence value is low because the action is already clear. At a cluttered intersection, evidence value is high because a small unseen detail can change whether the vehicle should yield, stop, or proceed.
The hybrid policy tries to estimate this quantity from scene complexity. When evidence value is high, the agent switches into active perception. When it is low, the agent keeps the fast path.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark scenes where another visual check is more valuable because the decision depends on details that may be easy to miss.

reads.html: Ask for more visual evidence only when that evidence is likely to change the driving choice.

Hybrid thinking succeeds when the policy can estimate scene complexity well enough to reserve active perception for cases where extra evidence improves grounding, because that keeps the expensive checks focused on the scenes where they can change the action.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: selective evidence gathering improves hard cases without slowing easy ones
paras: The method works because the cost of deeper perception is unevenly useful across scenes. A uniform always-check policy wastes time on easy examples, while an always-fast policy leaves hard examples underinformed. The hybrid switch finds a middle ground by spending the expensive visual check only where uncertainty is high.

Active perception also improves interpretability because the system can point to the specific visual evidence it requested before deciding. Cascaded RL helps train this behavior because the switch decision, the tool call, and the final driving action all influence the outcome, and the framework needs them to learn together.

stages.s: Estimate whether extra evidence is worth it
Call visual tools on complex scenes
Fast easy-case handling plus stronger hard-case grounding because complex scenes get extra evidence

math.h2: The decision rule: gather evidence when its value exceeds its cost
math.words: A simple formulation is to call the visual tool only when the expected decision improvement from extra evidence is larger than the cost of taking that extra perception step.
symbols: how much the extra visual evidence is expected to improve the driving decision
the delay or compute cost of gathering that evidence
the choice to invoke visual tools on the current scene

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Scene A is a clear open lane. Expected improvement from another visual check is small, say 1, while the cost is 3. The agent stays on the fast path.
Scene B is an occluded crosswalk. Expected improvement from another visual check is 7, while the cost is 3. The agent calls the visual tool.
The policy is useful because it spends effort where the scene can genuinely change the action.

math.note: The paper's reported gains fit this trade-off: selective active perception helps on long-tail complex scenes because those scenes need more evidence, while keeping the system practical for deployment because easy scenes skip the extra check.

bars.h2: The payoff: better hard-scene decisions with manageable cost

charts.title: Passive perception only
charts.note: A fast passive system handles ordinary scenes reasonably well but misses the details that decide many long-tail cases.

charts.title: DriveAgent-R1
charts.note: The paper reports competitive driving quality with a 3B model because active perception is reserved for scenes where deeper evidence has high value.

items.html: If the system treats a hard scene as easy, it will skip the visual check and may act on insufficient evidence.
If too many scenes trigger tool calls, the driving stack may become too slow for practical deployment.

Active perception helps only if the queried evidence matches the source of uncertainty, because only then does the extra check resolve the decision. A misplaced query adds cost without resolving the decision.

items.b: Done right: evidence gathering is selective and grounded.
items.html: The method succeeds when the agent calls visual tools on the scenes where one missing detail would change the driving action, because that is where the extra check pays for itself.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simulated driving task with two scene types: clear scenes where one forward view is enough, and ambiguous scenes where a targeted extra inspection reveals a hidden pedestrian, signal state, or lane boundary. Compare a passive planner against a planner that can decide whether to request another visual check. Record scene completion quality and average decision cost. The demo should show that the hybrid agent improves the ambiguous cases because it gathers the missing evidence before acting, while keeping easy scenes efficient by skipping unnecessary checks.
demo.closing: The demo must show that active perception is valuable because it is selective, not because the system simply spends more effort on every scene.
